The absorbing screen uses a third-order fractal Hilbert curve copper metal strip array combined with a CVD graphene sheet.
Graphene's surface impedance in the microwave band is tunable and nearly frequency-independent.
At 0 eV chemical potential, the absorption bandwidth is from 8.9 GHz to 18.1 GHz (relative bandwidth > 68%).
The central frequency of absorption can be tuned from 13.5 GHz to 19.0 GHz by changing graphene chemical potential from 0 to 0.4 eV.
The total thickness of the absorber is 3.4 mm, close to the theoretical minimum thickness limit of 3.1 mm for nonmagnetic absorbers.
The metal strips are made of copper with conductivity of 5.96×10^7 S/m and thickness of 5 μm.
Two extremely thin layers (50 nm silicon dioxide and 50 nm polysilicon) are placed under graphene to facilitate tunability.
The graphene sheet is directly underneath the metal strip array to maximize interaction and absorption.
The absorber is backed by a perfect electric conductor (PEC) ground to eliminate transmission.
Graphene conductivity changes from 0.9 mS to over 9 mS as chemical potential varies from 0 to 0.4 eV.
The surface resistance of graphene changes from about 1.2 kΩ at 0 eV to 110 Ω at 0.4 eV chemical potential.
The fractal Hilbert curve design provides multiple resonances enabling wideband impedance matching.
Without graphene, the absorber shows narrowband absorption peaks; graphene significantly broadens the absorption bandwidth.
The absorber maintains high absorption (>90%) over a wide frequency range with a low-profile thickness.
The chemical potential of graphene can be controlled by external DC bias voltage applied between graphene and polysilicon layer.
The effective absorption bandwidth decreases as chemical potential increases, from 9.2 GHz at 0 eV to 7.8 GHz at 0.4 eV.
The absorber's performance is robust against dielectric losses, indicating graphene is the main absorbing element.
Electric field distributions show strong field concentration near metal strips at resonance frequencies, enhancing absorption.
The carrier density in graphene is modulated by applied voltage, affecting chemical potential and conductivity.
The design uses CST Microwave Studio for optimization and simulation.
